transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-04-08 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~52 minutes | Attendees: Jordan Lee, Riya Patel, Samir Gupta (Redwood); Miguel Santos, Priya Kapoor, Evan Chu, Dana Li (Quantaco AI)

Summary: Quick recap of last week’s tests, deep dive on tokens/sec/$ numbers, caching and batching experiments, decision checklist for pilot expansion.

00:00:12 Jordan Lee: hey everyone thanks for joining on time, we'll kick off — quick round of intros?
00:00:20 Miguel Santos: Miguel here, head of ML at Quantaco, thanks Jordan.
00:00:23 Priya Kapoor: Priya, platform team.
00:00:25 Evan Chu: Evan, CTO.
00:00:27 Dana Li: Dana, SRE.
00:00:29 Riya Patel: Riya from Redwood, SE on the account, I'll lead the perf bits today.
00:00:33 Samir Gupta: Samir, helping with the cost models.
00:00:36 Jordan Lee: Great, agenda: 1) results recap 2) caching and batching deep dive 3) cost scenarios 4) next steps. Any additions?
00:00:44 Evan Chu: No, that's good. Looking for clear numbers on cost per 1M tokens and p99 latency impact.
00:00:50 Jordan Lee: Perfect, Riya over to you for the results.

00:01:05 Riya Patel: Okay so last week we ran three main experiments — baseline single-request (no batching) hosted quantized model, batching with batch size 8, and caching with prefix/KV enabled. We targeted the 70-token average response and a few 1k token tails as you asked. Numbers are rough but consistent across runs.
00:01:30 Riya Patel: Baseline hosted run: 1,200 tokens/sec sustained across cluster, cost math gives roughly $0.90 per 1M tokens on hosted at the current price tier we used for the POC. Batching x8: throughput jumps to ~6,000 tokens/sec but 95th latency for small interactive calls goes from ~180 ms to ~420 ms so tradeoff there. With KV prefix caching on repeated prompts we measured effective tokens/sec/user of ~3,500 on average because cache hits avoided re-computation for prefixes, which gives an effective unit cost of ~ $0.35 per 1M tokens for that workload mix.
00:02:20 Miguel Santos: Sorry can you repeat the cache number — $0.35?
00:02:24 Riya Patel: yeah about $0.35 per 1M tokens effective given your 60% prefix re-use in the sample traces you shared. That assumes a cache hit rate of 60% and average saved tokens of 40 tokens per hit.
00:02:36 Priya Kapoor: Our token distribution had a heavy tail — median 65 tokens, 95th 1,200 tokens. The cache hit was estimated from session-level repeated prompts, we’ll confirm.
00:02:45 Samir Gupta: Quick note on assumptions: our price per GPU-hour and token accounting used Redwood's dedicated pricing for variant A and hosted pricing for variant B; also we included an amortized storage cost for the KV cache but it's negligible at our scale.

00:03:05 Evan Chu: So batching increases throughput but hurts latency for interactive. Is there a hybrid approach?
00:03:12 Riya Patel: yes — we recommended adaptive batching in the doc: small requests go to low-latency pool (batch size 1-2) and background bulk inference uses larger batch sizes. Redwood routing can do policy-based routing by latency SLO and customer can pin a percentage of requests to dedicated low-latency nodes.
00:03:30 Jordan Lee: Also worth noting dedicated pools give more predictable tokens/sec/$ because of reserved GPU hours; hosted has burst advantages but higher marginal unit costs in our numbers.

00:04:00 Miguel Santos: Can you share the math for the $0.90 hosted per 1M tokens? I want the breakdown.
00:04:06 Samir Gupta: Sure, high level: we used the POC hosted rate tier of $X (internal) per vGPU-hour, the observed tokens/sec and concurrency over 1 hour, then divided to tokens per vGPU-hour and got the per million token number. I'll send a CSV with the inputs — but short version: baseline compute cost dominated, whereas with caching compute dropped ~60% effective.
00:04:30 Priya Kapoor: Do those hosted numbers include network and egress?
00:04:34 Samir Gupta: Not in this draft — we can add a conservative egress estimate. For inter-region it's material but for same-region customers it's small.

00:04:50 Riya Patel: I pulled some p99 numbers: for the quantized model we used for these runs p50 is ~80 ms, p90 ~180 ms, p99 ~480 ms in hosted baseline. With dedicated tuned kernels p99 falls to ~320 ms. When batching (x8) p99 goes to ~520-600 ms depending on queueing.
00:05:15 Dana Li: Interesting. We need p99 below 400 ms for the web UI paths. So dedicated looks necessary for those flows?
00:05:22 Riya Patel: For strict p99 < 400 ms for interactive endpoints, yes the recommendation is a dedicated low-latency pool with small batch sizes and some padding for KV cache warmups.

00:05:40 Miguel Santos: What about model quantization tradeoffs? We saw quality delta in our subjective evals.
00:05:46 Riya Patel: We tried Q4_0 quantization and Q5_0 variants — Q4 reduced latency by ~10-15% but introduced mild degradations on long-form coherence for a small subset of prompts. Q5 kept quality closer to FP16 but cost slightly higher. We can run targeted evals on your prompt set.

00:06:10 Evan Chu: Any fallback behavior if dedicated pool is saturated? We want graceful degradation.
00:06:15 Jordan Lee: Redwood routing supports fallback policies — can route to hosted lower-priority model variants or to smaller quantized variants. We can set multi-tier fallbacks to keep availability up while bounding cost.
00:06:28 Priya Kapoor: How do cache invalidations work with user-specific context?
00:06:32 Riya Patel: Cache is namespaced by session and can be configured with TTLs and versioning. For user-specific dynamic context we either skip prefix caching or aggressively shard keys. There is also a private-mode where we don't persist the keys beyond session life for privacy.

00:06:50 Miguel Santos: Let's dig into the saved tokens math — show me the example.
00:06:56 Riya Patel: Example from your sample trace: user issues same base prompt 3x across a session; each time we avoid ~40 tokens of recomputed prefix per request — at 60% hit rate across sessions we calculated approx 2.1M saved tokens per day on a 10k DAU workload which translates to roughly $x saved on hosted according to our previous rate. In dedicated the savings are dollar-savings on GPU hours and therefore even larger proportionally.
00:07:28 Samir Gupta: Also note cache hit behavior is workload dependent; if prompts are heavily personalized there may be less benefit. Your session reuse looked favorable though.

00:07:45 Miguel Santos: Can you run a sensitivity table — if cache hit is 40/50/60/70% what are our per-1M token costs?
00:07:52 Samir Gupta: Yes, that's part of the CSV I'll send. We already have a quick sensitivity: at 40% hit effective unit cost ~ $0.58, at 60% ~ $0.35, at 80% ~ $0.20 given current assumptions.

00:08:10 Priya Kapoor: For batching effects, what about time-of-day routing? Could we batch more during non-peak hours?
00:08:15 Riya Patel: Absolutely — that's recommended. Redwood supports scheduled scaling and routing by time windows. So non-peak batch sizes can be higher and you get bulk cost savings.

00:08:30 Dana Li: Any concerns about temperature with long sequences on dedicated GPUs? We saw throttling once in our infra months ago.
00:08:36 Riya Patel: We monitor utilization and have autoscaling rules. We also recommend spreading long-seq jobs across instances and using kernel compilation profiles tuned for long context so no single card thermal hotspot forms.

00:08:50 Evan Chu: What's the recommended split for interactive vs bulk in our POC?
00:08:54 Jordan Lee: From the numbers and your load profile I'd recommend 70% interactive on low-latency pool (small batch sizes, dedicated) and 30% bulk routed to larger batch size pools or hosted, adjustable once we see more production traces.

00:09:10 Miguel Santos: Timeline question — when can we make a call on expansion? We need numbers for the exec meeting next week.
00:09:16 Jordan Lee: We'll prioritize the cost model and the cached benchmark logs; Samir and Riya will finish by 4/12 so you should have everything in time for your exec review on 4/15.

00:09:30 Priya Kapoor: One more technical question — how do you handle KV eviction and consistency across rollouts?
00:09:36 Riya Patel: KV store uses LRU with configurable TTLs; during model rollouts we version keys and keep the older key namespace available for a short overlap period to avoid cold misses. We'll share the doc that outlines the rollout strategy.

00:09:52 Samir Gupta: Also flagging that if you choose aggressive quantization we should run quality gates in CI, Redwood can integrate evals into your pipeline to detect regressions.

00:10:05 Miguel Santos: Good. Let's go through the cost scenarios quickly — host vs dedicated vs hybrid with numbers.
00:10:10 Samir Gupta: Scenario A (hosted): $0.90 per 1M tokens baseline, with worst-case p99 ~480 ms. Scenario B (dedicated): amortized unit cost ~$0.60 per 1M tokens because of reserved hours, p99 ~320 ms with tuned kernels. Scenario C (hybrid + caching): with 60% cache hit and 70/30 split interactive/bulk, effective unit cost ~$0.28 per 1M tokens and p99 for interactive portion ~340 ms. These are illustrative and we'll provide CSV.
00:10:52 Evan Chu: Those numbers are promising if the hybrid holds. How confident are you in the 60% cache hit?
00:10:58 Riya Patel: Based on your provided sample traces it was 55-65% across sessions; Priya will verify on a larger window.

00:11:10 Priya Kapoor: We'll run a 2-week log sweep and share the distribution by 4/11.

00:11:18 Jordan Lee: Great — operational asks: we will prepare a small ops runbook: how to configure adaptive batching, cache TTLs, routing policies, and fallback policies. Samir will include cost assumptions and sensitivity.

00:11:34 Miguel Santos: Any security/compliance impacts for caching? We have PII in some prompts.
00:11:40 Riya Patel: Cache can be set to not persist PII or to encrypt keys with your KMS; for Private deployment we also support customer-managed keys and audit logs. We'll send the security docs link.

00:11:55 Dana Li: Good. For our decision we also need a failure-mode analysis — if cache node fails what does request latency look like?
00:12:02 Samir Gupta: Fallback is to compute path, so latency temporarily rises to baseline, but routing can divert traffic to alternate nodes; we'll include an outage run scenario in the doc.

00:12:18 Jordan Lee: Any other questions from the customer side?
00:12:21 Evan Chu: Not right now.

00:12:25 Jordan Lee: Ok we'll open the floor for open discussion, otherwise quick recap and next steps.

00:12:33 Miguel Santos: One practical ask — can we get a short video showing the toggles for batching and cache in the console? Engineers like seeing the UI.
00:12:40 Samir Gupta: Samir will record a short 3-minute clip and attach.

00:12:46 Riya Patel: One technical note — when you test at scale, try to preserve the session patterns. Synthetic replay that doesn't model prefix reuse will understate caching benefits.

00:12:58 Priya Kapoor: Noted. We'll run the replay tool with session affinity.

00:13:05 Jordan Lee: Recap of next steps: Jordan sends cost model CSV, Riya runs cached benchmark and shares logs, Priya shares token distribution, Samir records video and compiles sensitivity table. Action owners and dates in the notes.

00:13:20 Miguel Santos: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.

00:13:25 Jordan Lee: Thanks all. We'll follow up in Slack and send the deck and CSV after the call.

00:13:30 Meeting ends — small post-call chatter omitted.

Notes about transcript quality: occasional mis-heard words and shorthand abbreviations; speakers sometimes overlap; timestamps approximate every ~15-60 seconds. Logs and CSVs to be attached separately (links will be emailed).
